what_it_does: Many AI models — recommendation systems (like those that suggest what to buy or watch) and large language models — rely on lookup tables called embedding tables: giant arrays where each row is a dense numerical description of a concept such as a user ID or a word. When the model looks up a row in such a table, the memory address it accesses reveals which user or which word is being processed, creating a privacy leak through what security researchers call a side-channel: an attacker who can observe the pattern of memory accesses (even without reading the data itself) can infer sensitive inputs. Standard privacy-preserving defenses for memory accesses — called Oblivious RAM (ORAM), which shuffles and encrypts accesses so observers cannot tell what was looked up — are far too slow for the massive embedding tables used in practice. This paper evaluates three alternative approaches: scanning the entire table every time (so all rows are accessed regardless of which one is needed, hiding the answer in the crowd); using optimized ORAM; and replacing the table entirely with a small neural network that computes an embedding on the fly from a hash of the index, so no revealing memory lookup ever occurs. A hybrid strategy mixes these approaches, choosing the cheapest option for each individual table based on its size.
